methods.label: Recover the earlier factors
methods.explanation:
A product divided by one nonzero factor gives the other factor, so the known ending lets us work backward. Let \(a_k\) be the number in position \(k\). For example, \(a_7=a_5a_6\), so \(a_5=64\div16\). Repeating this reasoning gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5&=64\div16=4,\\
a_4&=16\div4=4,\\
a_3&=4\div4=1,\\
a_2&=4\div1=4,\\
a_1&=1\div4=\frac14.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every divisor is positive, so each step forces a unique earlier value. The resulting list is
\[
\frac14,\ 4,\ 1,\ 4,\ 4,\ 16,\ 64,\ 1024.
\]
The final multiplication \(16\cdot64=1024\) also holds, so the entire list satisfies the rule. The first number is \(\frac14\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
